definition: A set of vertices joined by edges; only which vertices are joined matters, not where they are drawn or how long the edges look.
One of the points of a graph, also called a node, which edges join to other vertices.
A line in a graph joining two vertices, or joining a vertex to itself, in which case it is called a loop.
The number of edge ends at a vertex, with a loop counting twice; in any graph the degrees add up to twice the number of edges.
A graph with no loops and no multiple edges, so each pair of vertices is joined by at most one edge.
A simple graph in which every pair of vertices is joined by an edge; the complete graph $K_n$ on $n$ vertices has $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ edges.
A graph with a number, called a weight, on each edge, standing for something such as a distance, time or cost.
A graph in which you can travel along edges from any vertex to any other vertex.
A directed graph in which you can travel from every vertex to every other vertex following the directions of the edges.
A graph in which each edge has a direction, shown by an arrow, and is travelled only that way; a vertex's in-degree counts edges coming in and its out-degree counts edges going out.
A graph made from some of the vertices and edges of another graph, in which every chosen edge keeps both of its end vertices.
A connected graph with no cycles; a tree with $n$ vertices has $n - 1$ edges.
